In https://github.com/leanprover-community/plausible/pull/80 @Mike Hicks made the suggestion to have plausible's deriving handler support the following scenario:

structure Params where
  Meta : Type
  IDMeta : Type

inductive Bar (T : Params) where
  | mk : T.Meta → T.IDMeta → Bar T

deriving instance Arbitrary for Bar

By requiring instances on the types contained in Params. This is a pattern used in e.g. strata here. Does this seem like a technique that deriving handlers should support in general? Is there a nice way to refactor most of our deriving handlers to just handle this?

Looks somewhat idiosyncratic to me, not sure if it makes sense to support all ways where users can hide type parameters in our deriving handlers.

In Haskell the problem is “solved” by allowing users to write the full instance signature, and still derive the methods. This way the handlers don't have to guess the assumptions of the instance. We don't have that ability, do we?

Looks somewhat idiosyncratic to me, ...

So is the implication that this approach to parameterization is an anti-pattern? Or that parameterization is an anti pattern in general? I'd love to leverage deriving handlers whenever possible, rather than write by-hand versions that basically do what the deriving ones already do, almost. Maybe there is a different parameterization pattern that we could see deriving handlers supporting?

@Joe Hendrix recommended this approach in Strata based on his experience presented in this paper.  It discusses some of the parameterized programming used at Galois in Crucible for more type-safe program transformations. In particular, they wrote the template Haskell for deriving traversals and other basic operations over parameterized type classes in this module.

That style was really useful for embedding typed languages in Haskell. For example in Crucible (baring unsafeCoerce or dynamic checks), expressions were embeded in Haskell using parametered types, so that it was, for example impossible to accidentally build an add expression with mismatched types.

At the time, I was a little unsure whether it was worth the added annotation overhead, but now that i've worked with untyped expressions more, I am convinced it was. It's just too easy to forget an explicit cast or runcheck particularly with LLM generated code.
I've found this kind of parameterization very useful. It would be great to support it in deriving in some way, even if it requires additional annotations.

Joachim Breitner said:

In Haskell the problem is “solved” by allowing users to write the full instance signature, and still derive the methods.

This could be nice with syntax like this:

deriving instance Repr for Bar T with [Repr T.Meta] [Repr T.IDMeta]

Here's a potential pattern to work around this limitation:

inductive T₀ (α β : Type)
deriving Repr

structure Sig where (α β : Type)
abbrev T (S : Sig) := T₀ S.α S.β

#synth Repr (T ⟨Nat, Nat⟩) -- ✓
#lean4 > RFC: `deriving Repr` should add `Repr` binders seems relevant here

That does seem relevant. One issue that came up at Galois is the need to be type directed on sub arguments. It used TemplateHaskelll. Here's an example showing a more complex traversal:

{-# LANGUAGE GADTs #-}
{-# LANGUAGE TemplateHaskell #-}
{-# LANGUAGE RankNTypes #-}
{-# LANGUAGE KindSignatures #-}
{-# LANGUAGE DataKinds #-}

import Data.Parameterized.TH.GADT
import Data.Parameterized.TraversableF
import Data.Parameterized.Classes

-- 1. A secondary parameterized type that needs its own traversal logic
data SubComponent (tp :: *) where
  SubInt  :: Int -> SubComponent Int
  SubBool :: Bool -> SubComponent Bool

-- Assume TraversableF is already derived for SubComponent
$(structuralTraversal ''SubComponent [])

-- 2. Our primary GADT that requires custom traversal logic
data MyExpr (tp :: *) where
  -- Scenario A: A normal field with the parameter type
  BaseCase :: tp -> MyExpr tp

  -- Scenario B: A standard Haskell type wrapping the parameter type (Needs Override)
  ManyVals :: [tp] -> MyExpr tp

  -- Scenario C: A different GADT wrapping the parameter type (Needs Override)
  Nested   :: SubComponent tp -> MyExpr tp

-- 3. Define the structural traversal with customized type overrides
$(structuralTraversalWithOverrides ''MyExpr
    [ -- Override for standard lists: use the standard traverse function
      ( [t| [] |], [| traverse |])
    , -- Override for the secondary GADT: use its TraversableF instance function
      ( [t| SubComponent |], [| traverseF |])
    ]
 )

We could probably make this a lot more ergonomic, but this macro was really useful for dealing with large parameterized IRs.

@Joe Hendrix I'm revisiting this thread and honestly I am not getting your followup. I am not a template Haskell guy.

I like @Eric Wieser 's observation about "late binding" for nested types, but I'm not sure how it applies in this case.

@Francisco Giordano 's workaround seems like it captures what I was looking for, originally. Do you think, Joe, that Strata's defs could follow that pattern instead, and therefore avail themselves to the built-in deriving machinery better?

@Mike Hicks I think that should work.

I reread what I wrote and I think I explained the limitation badly. This affected Crucible, but I don't know if will affect Strata Core in the same way.

To understand the Crucible issue, Let's suppose we have a "dependent list". In this case, lets assume we have a list K : List α and a function f : α → Type, we want a list DepList K f with length K.length and whose i'th element has type f K[i]. To derive a Repr instance for DepList, we need a polymorphic repr constraint like ∀(a : α), Repr (f a) rather than a single constraint like Repr α.

The Haskell parameterized utils package had some utilities for working with these constraints. That was important for Crucible since it had some optimizations so that symbolic value representations were type directed (e.g., Crucible's symbolic representation of a heap was quite different from a Integer), and we had lists for typing contexts with dependent lists for the symbolic values. Strata doesn't have this.

Is that explanation more clear? The TLDR is that quantifying over constraints introduces additional complexity.
